samples.text:
Nowadays, some countries invite skilled workers from other countries to come and live there because they do not have enough workers in some jobs. In my opinion, this policy has more advantages than disadvantages for the receiving country.

The first and most important advantage is that it solve the problem of labour shortages. For example, many countries do not have enough doctors, nurses or engineers, and training new people takes many years. When skilled workers come from abroad, hospitals and companies can continue to work well. Also, these workers pay taxes, which help the government to pay for public services like schools and pensions. This is very important in countries where the population is getting older and there is fewer young workers. In addition, people from different countries bring new ideas and cultures, which can make the society more interesting.

However, there are also some disadvantages. Some local workers may feel that the newcomers are taking their jobs or that they reduce the salaries. This can cause tension between local people and the new arrivals. Moreover, the new workers need houses, schools for their children and health services, so there can be more pressure on these services. Another problem is that the government may not train its own citizens because it is easier to bring workers from other country.

In conclusion, encouraging skilled workers from abroad can cause some problems such as tension and pressure on public services. However, I think the benefits for the economy and important services like health care is bigger. So the advantages outweigh the disadvantages, but the government should also invest in training local people.
samples.why: Clear judgement for the receiving country · relevant ideas but support is general and somewhat repetitive · mechanical linking · adequate vocabulary · several agreement and article errors that do not impede meaning.

samples.text:
Faced with shortages in key professions, a number of countries actively encourage qualified workers from overseas to settle permanently. Although this approach can create some social and economic challenges, I believe it brings greater benefits to the receiving country.

The most direct advantage is that skilled migrants fill gaps that cannot be filled quickly from within the domestic workforce. Training a doctor or an engineer can take many years, whereas recruiting experienced professionals from abroad allows hospitals, construction projects and technology firms to operate effectively in the meantime. This helps to maintain the quality of public services and prevents businesses from losing opportunities because they lack staff. Furthermore, many developed countries have ageing populations, and working-age migrants contribute taxes that help fund pensions and healthcare for older citizens. Skilled newcomers can also bring fresh ideas and international connections, which may stimulate innovation.

However, there are some potential drawbacks. If large numbers of people arrive in a short period, they can put pressure on housing, schools and transport, particularly in major cities where most newcomers tend to settle. There may also be concerns among local workers that competition from abroad will reduce wages or limit their own job opportunities, which can lead to social tension if it is not managed carefully. In addition, relying on foreign recruitment may reduce the incentive for governments and employers to invest in training their own citizens.

These disadvantages, though, can be managed through sensible planning. Governments can match recruitment to genuine shortages, invest in infrastructure where newcomers settle and continue funding domestic training programmes at the same time.

In conclusion, while attracting skilled workers from abroad can strain public services and cause some local resentment, its contribution to filling vital roles and supporting an ageing population make it highly beneficial. On balance, the advantages outweigh the disadvantages.
samples.why: Clear position throughout · main ideas extended and supported, with sensible mitigation · clear topic in each paragraph · good range of vocabulary (ageing populations, domestic workforce) · mostly error-free, one agreement slip.

samples.text:
Many economies now rely on targeted immigration schemes to attract qualified professionals from abroad, particularly in sectors such as healthcare, engineering and technology. Although this strategy is not without complications, I would argue that, for the receiving country, its advantages clearly outweigh its disadvantages.

The most compelling benefit is the speed with which skills gaps can be closed. Domestic training pipelines take years to respond to changes in demand, and in the meantime shortages of nurses or software engineers can lengthen waiting lists, delay infrastructure projects and deter investment. Recruiting professionals who are already qualified allows these needs to be met almost immediately, and without the host country bearing the cost of their education. Skilled migrants also tend to be of working age and in well-paid employment, so they make a substantial contribution to public finances, which is increasingly valuable in societies where a shrinking workforce must support a growing number of retirees. Moreover, diverse teams often bring new perspectives, languages and international networks that strengthen innovation and trade.

The disadvantages are nonetheless significant. Rapid population growth in particular regions can outpace the supply of housing and school places, and if this pressure coincides with stagnant wages in some sectors, it can fuel resentment and social division. Employers may also come to regard overseas recruitment as a cheaper alternative to developing local talent, leaving domestic workers without opportunities to acquire in-demand skills. Finally, successful integration requires sustained investment in language support and the recognition of foreign qualifications, without which highly trained migrants may end up underemployed.

Crucially, these problems stem mainly from poor planning rather than from skilled migration itself, and they can be addressed through coordinated housing policy, parallel investment in domestic training and effective integration programmes.

In conclusion, attracting skilled workers from abroad carries social and practical challenges, but its contribution to essential services, public finances and economic dynamism means that its advantages outweigh its disadvantages for the receiving country.
samples.why: Fully addresses the question from the receiving country's perspective with a clear judgement · ideas well developed and logically sequenced · wide, precise vocabulary (skills gaps, underemployed) · wide range of error-free structures.
